Breeding data and relationship matrices

Muhammad Farooqi

Source: vignettes/BreedingExperiment.Rmd
BreedingExperiment.Rmd

Why this package

A quantitative-genetic analysis needs four things at once: the marker genotypes, the phenotypes, the pedigree, and where the markers sit on the genome. Keeping them in four separate objects is where mistakes creep in, as soon as one of them is filtered or reordered. Drop a marker from the genotype matrix and the map no longer lines up; reorder the phenotypes and every breeding value is attached to the wrong animal. Nothing warns you.

Bioconductor solved that problem generally with SummarizedExperiment, and BreedingExperiment applies the solution to breeding data. It extends RangedSummarizedExperiment, so markers are rows, individuals are columns, and marker positions are a GRanges. Subsetting takes the genotypes, the phenotypes, the marker coordinates and the pedigree with it. Everything you already know about Bioconductor containers applies.

The relationship matrices are then methods on that container rather than free-standing functions fed loose matrices:

  • Amatrix(), the pedigree numerator relationship matrix;
  • Gmatrix(), the genomic relationship matrix;
  • Dmatrix(), the dominance relationship matrix;
  • Hmatrix(), the single-step matrix combining pedigree and markers.

That last one is the reason the package exists. Real breeding programmes genotype only part of the population, and single-step genomic prediction is how the genotyped and ungenotyped parts are analysed together.

What else is available

It is worth being specific about what this package adds, because the individual matrices are not new.

On Bioconductor, relatedness is available from two directions, but never both at once:

Package What it gives you
SNPRelate snpgdsGRM(), a genomic relationship matrix from GDS-backed genotypes, and IBD and PCA analyses. Scales far past this package, with no pedigree.
GENESIS PC-AiR and PC-Relate, kinship estimated from markers while adjusting for ancestry, plus mixed-model association testing.
GeneticsPed Pedigree classes, relationship and inbreeding coefficients. Pedigree only; its own description notes that it is not stable.
Pedixplorer Pedigree objects, kinship matrices and pedigree drawing, succeeding kinship2. Pedigree only.
FamAgg Pedigree handling and tests of familial aggregation of traits. Pedigree only.

So Bioconductor can give you relationships from a pedigree, or relationships from markers, but not a container that holds both kinds of data together and not the single-step matrix that reconciles them.

On CRAN, AGHmatrix is the closest relative and in some ways goes further than this package. It computes A, G, dominance and H matrices, it covers autopolyploids as well as diploids, it offers several parameterisations of each matrix, and it is compiled, so it is faster. What it does not do is hold your data: it takes loose matrices and data frames and returns loose matrices, leaving the genotypes, pedigree, phenotypes and map for you to keep aligned. The differences worth knowing are:

  • Orientation. AGHmatrix::Gmatrix() expects individuals in rows and markers in columns. This package follows the Bioconductor convention and puts markers in rows.
  • Single-step. AGHmatrix::Hmatrix() takes an already-computed A and G and offers the Martini and Munoz methods. Hmatrix() here works from the object, and uses the tuning and blending described below.
  • Dominance. AGHmatrix reaches dominance through Gmatrix(method = "Vitezica"); here it is Dmatrix().
  • Names. AGHmatrix also exports Amatrix, Gmatrix and Hmatrix, so loading both packages masks whichever was loaded first. Use BreedingExperiment::Gmatrix() if you need both in one session.

Choose AGHmatrix if you work on autopolyploids or want its alternative parameterisations; choose SNPRelate if you have hundreds of thousands of samples and no pedigree; choose this package if your data belong in a Bioconductor container and you want the single-step matrix.

Two limitations are worth stating plainly. The relationship matrices are dense base-R matrices, which suits thousands of individuals rather than hundreds of thousands. And the package estimates no variance components and fits no association tests: it produces the relationship structures, and a solver consumes them, as shown at the end of this vignette.

Installation 

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("BreedingExperiment")

The development version lives on GitHub:

BiocManager::install("mqfarooqi1/BreedingExperiment")
library(BreedingExperiment)

The demonstration data

The package ships with demoBreeding, a simulated five-generation population built to behave like a real programme rather than a textbook example.

data(demoBreeding)
be <- demoBreeding
be
#> class: BreedingExperiment
#> markers: 900  individuals genotyped: 120 
#> assays(1): genotype
#> phenotypes(6): generation sex yield stature trueBV_yield trueBV_stature
#> sequences(10): chr1 chr2 chr3 chr4 chr5 chr6
#> pedigree: 180 individuals (120 genotyped, 60 not; 30 founders)

Read the last line carefully: the pedigree describes 180 individuals but only 120 were genotyped. The two earliest generations were born before genotyping began. That is the normal situation in a breeding programme, and it is the reason Hmatrix() exists.

The data also carry the other awkward features of real records: a trait measured on one sex only, a little missing genotype data, and unequal family sizes because a few sires were used heavily.

table(SummarizedExperiment::colData(be)$generation)
#> 
#>  3  4  5 
#> 35 40 45
summary(SummarizedExperiment::colData(be)$yield)   # females only
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#>    4203    5605    5934    6000    6278    8097      54

If you would rather generate your own population, simulateBreeding() does that.

The standard accessors work:

dim(be)
#> [1] 900 120
genotypes(be)[1:4, 1:5]
#>          C0001 C0002 C0003 C0004 C0005
#> snp00001     2     2     1     1     2
#> snp00002     1     0     2     1     1
#> snp00003     2     2     2     1     1
#> snp00004     2     1     2     1     0
head(SummarizedExperiment::colData(be), 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 6 columns
#>       generation      sex     yield   stature trueBV_yield trueBV_stature
#>        <integer> <factor> <numeric> <numeric>    <numeric>      <numeric>
#> C0001          3        M        NA     158.3      -0.3883         1.5128
#> C0002          3        M        NA     139.3       0.8635        -0.5965
#> C0003          3        M        NA     129.0      -0.3502        -1.7890
head(pedigree(be), 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 3 columns
#>            id        sire         dam
#>   <character> <character> <character>
#> 1       A0001          NA          NA
#> 2       A0002          NA          NA
#> 3       A0003          NA          NA

Because markers are genomic ranges, a data set can be cut down to a region:

chr1 <- be[as.character(GenomicRanges::seqnames(
  SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(be))) == "chr1", ]
dim(chr1)
#> [1]  90 120

Building an object from your own data

Your own data goes in the same way:

be <- BreedingExperiment(
  genotypes  = dosage_matrix,          # markers x individuals, 0/1/2
  phenotypes = phenotype_data_frame,   # one row per individual
  pedigree   = pedigree_data_frame,    # id, sire, dam
  rowRanges  = marker_granges)         # optional, but worth having

Two habits are worth forming. Give phenotypes row names that are the individual identifiers, and they will be matched by name rather than by position; row names that do not match the genotype column names are an error rather than something quietly overwritten. And pass real rowRanges whenever you have them, because that is what makes a data set subsettable by genomic region.

The pedigree may name ancestors that were never genotyped, which is exactly what Hmatrix() needs. Parents that never appear in the id column are added as founders, and unknown parents may be written NA or 0.

Quality control 

nrow(be)
#> [1] 900
summary(alleleFrequency(be)$callRate)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.9583  0.9833  0.9917  0.9900  1.0000  1.0000

Take the marker summaries before imputing. callRate counts dosages that are present, so after imputation it is 1 everywhere; observed heterozygosity, by contrast, ignores imputed cells and is unaffected.

be <- filterMarkers(be, min_maf = 0.05, min_call_rate = 0.9)
be <- imputeMarkers(be)
nrow(be)
#> [1] 801
head(alleleFrequency(be), 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 4 columns
#>               freq       maf  callRate heterozygosity
#>          <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>      <numeric>
#> snp00001  0.707627 0.2923729         1       0.483051
#> snp00002  0.605932 0.3940678         1       0.516949
#> snp00003  0.920168 0.0798319         1       0.159664

Choosing the thresholds

min_maf and min_call_rate are judgement calls, not constants of nature. Common starting points are a minor allele frequency between 0.01 and 0.05 and a call rate between 0.90 and 0.95. Raise min_maf when the panel is large and the sample small, because an allele seen in one or two individuals says almost nothing about relationships while still adding noise; lower it when rare variants are the point of the study. Filter before imputing, so that imputation is not asked to rescue markers that should simply be discarded.

How much this matters is worth checking rather than assuming:

# on the unfiltered data, so that every threshold has markers to remove
round(t(vapply(c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20), function(m) {
  G <- Gmatrix(demoBreeding, min_maf = m)
  c(min_maf = m, mean_diagonal = mean(diag(G)),
    sd_offdiagonal = stats::sd(G[upper.tri(G)]))
}, numeric(3))), 3)
#>      min_maf mean_diagonal sd_offdiagonal
#> [1,]    0.00         0.965          0.117
#> [2,]    0.01         0.965          0.117
#> [3,]    0.05         0.964          0.117
#> [4,]    0.20         0.963          0.120

imputeMarkers() fills missing dosages with twice the allele frequency and records which cells it filled in an imputed assay, carried through subsetting with everything else:

SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(be)
#> [1] "genotype" "imputed"
mean(SummarizedExperiment::assay(be, "imputed"))   # proportion imputed
#> [1] 0.01014357

That is adequate for the low missingness left after filtering. For anything more, impute with dedicated software and pass the expected dosages in directly; the container accepts values between 0 and 2.

Relationships from the pedigree

Amatrix() builds the numerator relationship matrix. Its entries are the familiar textbook values: one half between parent and offspring, one quarter between grandparent and grandchild.

A <- Amatrix(be)
round(A[1:5, 1:5], 3)
#>       A0001 A0002 A0003 A0004 A0005
#> A0001     1     0     0     0     0
#> A0002     0     1     0     0     0
#> A0003     0     0     1     0     0
#> A0004     0     0     0     1     0
#> A0005     0     0     0     0     1

The diagonal carries inbreeding:

summary(inbreeding(be))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> 0.00000 0.00000 0.00000 0.03941 0.06445 0.18750

Relationships from the markers

Gmatrix() is the genomic relationship matrix. It measures what actually happened rather than what was expected: two full sibs have a pedigree relationship of exactly 0.5, but their genomic relationship varies around it, because Mendelian sampling gave them different halves of their parents.

G <- Gmatrix(be)
round(G[1:5, 1:5], 3)
#>        C0001  C0002  C0003  C0004  C0005
#> C0001  0.962  0.016 -0.112 -0.165 -0.184
#> C0002  0.016  1.094 -0.056 -0.073  0.057
#> C0003 -0.112 -0.056  1.143  0.080  0.099
#> C0004 -0.165 -0.073  0.080  1.002  0.057
#> C0005 -0.184  0.057  0.099  0.057  1.078

The two agree in the aggregate, which is a useful sanity check on any data set:

gen <- colnames(be)
A22 <- A[gen, gen]
cor(A22[upper.tri(A22)], G[upper.tri(G)])
#> [1] 0.8661597
plot(A22[upper.tri(A22)], G[upper.tri(G)], pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
     col = grDevices::adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.3),
     xlab = "pedigree relationship", ylab = "genomic relationship")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

Pedigree and genomic relationships for the same pairs of individuals. The pedigree gives a few discrete values; the markers spread each of them out, and that spread is the Mendelian sampling a pedigree cannot see.

Dmatrix() gives the dominance relationships, orthogonal to the additive ones, for models that separate the two:

D <- Dmatrix(be)
round(D[1:4, 1:4], 3)
#>        C0001  C0002  C0003  C0004
#> C0001  0.982 -0.024 -0.059 -0.066
#> C0002 -0.024  1.148 -0.094  0.025
#> C0003 -0.059 -0.094  1.138  0.004
#> C0004 -0.066  0.025  0.004  0.972

Combining both: the single-step matrix

Using only G discards every ungenotyped relative. Using only A discards the markers. Hmatrix() keeps both, and covers every individual in the pedigree:

H <- Hmatrix(be, blend = 0.05)
dim(H)
#> [1] 180 180
length(attr(H, "genotyped"))
#> [1] 120

The genotyped block comes from the markers, the ungenotyped block from the pedigree corrected by what the markers say about genotyped relatives, and the off-diagonal blocks connect them. Two checks confirm the behaviour: blending entirely towards the pedigree returns A22, and the result stays positive definite.

H1 <- Hmatrix(be, blend = 1, tune = FALSE)
max(abs(H1[gen, gen] - A22))
#> [1] 0
min(eigen(H, only.values = TRUE)$values) > 0
#> [1] TRUE

Choosing blend and tune

Leave tune = TRUE unless you have already put G on the scale of A22 yourself. Untuned, the two matrices usually disagree about the average level of relationship, and that disagreement is passed straight into the ungenotyped block, where it appears as breeding values biased between the genotyped and ungenotyped groups.

blend has two jobs. A small weight on A22 makes the genotyped block invertible, which matters whenever there are fewer markers than genotyped individuals, and it pulls the markers back towards the pedigree where the marker estimate is noisy. Values between 0.01 and 0.10 are usual and 0.05 is a reasonable default: use 0.05 to 0.10 for a small marker panel and 0.01 to 0.02 for a dense one on many individuals. blend = 0 keeps G as it is and will fail if G is singular; blend = 1 discards the markers altogether.

With 801 markers on 120 individuals the choice makes very little difference here, which is itself the point: blending matters most when G is close to singular.

vapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.20), function(b) {
  Hb <- Hmatrix(be, blend = b)
  min(eigen(Hb, only.values = TRUE)$values)
}, numeric(1))
#> [1] 0.07095017 0.07216610 0.07713689

A complete example: single-step BLUP

The matrices are not the end of an analysis, so here is what you do with one. These are Henderson’s mixed model equations for a single random genetic effect, y=Xb+Zu+e,u∼N(0,Kσu2),e∼N(0,Iσe2),y = Xb + Zu + e, \qquad u \sim N(0, K\sigma^2_u), \qquad e \sim N(0, I\sigma^2_e), solved directly with λ=σe2/σu2\lambda = \sigma^2_e / \sigma^2_u: [X′XX′ZZ′XZ′Z+K−1λ][bu]=[X′yZ′y].\begin{bmatrix} X'X & X'Z \\ Z'X & Z'Z + K^{-1}\lambda \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} b \\ u \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X'y \\ Z'y \end{bmatrix}.

Put H in for KK and the solution covers every individual in the pedigree, genotyped or not. The validation is the one a breeder actually cares about: hide the records of the youngest generation, predict their breeding values from their parents and their markers, and see how well the predictions correlate with the truth that the simulation knows.

ph  <- SummarizedExperiment::colData(be)
ids <- rownames(H)

train  <- ph$generation != 5                 # records we are allowed to use
target <- colnames(be)[ph$generation == 5]   # the ones we must predict
y <- ph$stature[train]

X <- matrix(1, length(y), 1)                 # an intercept only
Z <- matrix(0, length(y), length(ids))       # records to individuals
Z[cbind(seq_along(y), match(colnames(be)[train], ids))] <- 1
c(records = length(y), predicted = length(target))
#>   records predicted 
#>        75        45
blup <- function(K, h2) {
  lambda <- (1 - h2) / h2
  lhs <- rbind(cbind(crossprod(X),    crossprod(X, Z)),
               cbind(crossprod(Z, X), crossprod(Z) + solve(K) * lambda))
  rhs <- rbind(crossprod(X, y), crossprod(Z, y))
  stats::setNames(solve(lhs, rhs)[-1, 1], ids)
}

ebv_pedigree   <- blup(A[ids, ids], h2 = 0.6)
ebv_singlestep <- blup(H,           h2 = 0.6)

stature was simulated with a heritability of 0.6, which is the value used here. In a real analysis the variance components are estimated, by REML in a package such as sommer, rrBLUP, BGLR or lme4qtl, or by standalone software such as ASReml or BLUPF90; all of them accept a relationship matrix or its inverse, which is what this package produces.

true <- stats::setNames(ph$trueBV_stature, colnames(be))
round(c(pedigree   = cor(ebv_pedigree[target],   true[target]),
        singlestep = cor(ebv_singlestep[target], true[target])), 3)
#>   pedigree singlestep 
#>      0.410      0.435

Adding the markers raises the correlation with the true breeding values of the unrecorded generation. The gain is real but modest, and that is honest for this data set: the simulated pedigree is complete and error-free, which is the situation in which a pedigree-only analysis does best. The advantage of single-step grows as pedigrees become incomplete and as more records accumulate on ungenotyped relatives.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (nm in c("pedigree", "singlestep")) {
  e <- if (nm == "pedigree") ebv_pedigree else ebv_singlestep
  plot(true[target], e[target], pch = 16, col = "steelblue",
       xlab = "true breeding value", ylab = "predicted",
       main = sprintf("%s (r = %.3f)", nm, cor(e[target], true[target])))
  abline(lm(e[target] ~ true[target]), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}

Predicted against true breeding values for the youngest generation, whose records were withheld. Adding marker information tightens the relationship. 

par(op)

The other half of what H buys you is easy to miss: the 60 ungenotyped ancestors get predictions too, on the same scale, from one solve.

ungenotyped <- setdiff(ids, attr(H, "genotyped"))
length(ungenotyped)
#> [1] 60
summary(ebv_singlestep[ungenotyped])
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> -7.4187 -1.9093 -0.3128 -0.6866  0.3059  5.4087
